q1: False. <!DOCTYPE html> is not an HTML element and does not require a closing tag. It's a special instruction to the browser.
q2: The browser renders in quirks mode. Without the doctype, browsers use legacy compatibility mode that can cause inconsistent rendering.
q3: <head>. The head element contains machine-readable metadata like title, meta tags, and links to CSS, which are not displayed directly on the page.
q4: One. A valid HTML document should have exactly one <body> element that contains all the visible content.
q5: It causes inconsistent rendering and box-model behavior. Standards mode ensures consistent rendering across browsers, while quirks mode mimics old browser behavior.
q6: html → head → body. The correct order is: <!DOCTYPE html>, then <html> as the root, containing <head> first, then <body>.
q7: Contains metadata about the document. The <head> element holds information like title, meta tags, and links to external resources, not visible content.
q8: Visible and interactive content. The <body> element contains everything the user sees and interacts with: text, images, forms, etc.
q9: Browsers may silently move it to <body> or ignore it. Putting visible content in <head> is invalid, and browsers may attempt to fix it, but you shouldn't rely on this.
q10: To tell the browser to render in standards mode. The doctype instruction switches the browser from legacy quirks mode to modern standards mode.
